matching has all of its matching edges forcing; and forcing is symmetric in its
endpoints. We then explain how this local reduction is the engine behind a
structural dichotomy for \emph{bricks}: apart from three classical exceptions --
the tetrahedron $K_4$, the complement of the six-cycle $\Cbar$, and the Petersen
graph -- a brick has the property that every \emph{b-invariant edge} is forcing
if and only if it is a near-bipartite brick in the explicitly characterised
family. All results are stated with full proof sketches and are self-contained;
no finiteness assumption is needed for the core deletion theorem.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph. A \emph{perfect matching} of $G$ is a set of
edges $M\subseteq E$ such that every vertex is incident to exactly one edge of
$M$. Within a graph that admits perfect matchings, an edge $e$ is a
\emph{forcing edge} if precisely one perfect matching contains $e$; committing
to a forcing edge determines the whole matching. Forcing edges are the rigid,
choice-free constraints inside an otherwise flexible object, and identifying
them recurs in matching theory, in the study of Kekul\'e structures in
chemistry, and in the theory of \emph{bricks}.

This paper has two goals: to establish cleanly the local \emph{deletion
characterisation} of forcing edges, and to explain how that characterisation
functions as the reduction step in a structural \emph{dichotomy theorem} for
bricks, relating forcing to near-bipartiteness up to three classical
exceptional graphs.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
  \item A model of perfect matchings as fixed-point-free involutions
        (Section~\ref{sec:model}) that turns ``the matching containing $uv$''
        into the equation $f(u)=v$.
  \item The deletion characterisation (Theorem~\ref{thm:deletion}): $uv$ is
        forcing iff $uv$ is an edge and $G-u-v$ has a unique perfect matching.
  \item Three companion results: the interior-avoidance lemma
        (Lemma~\ref{lem:avoid}), the completeness principle
        (Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}), and the symmetry of forcing
        (Theorem~\ref{thm:sym}).
  \item An exposition (Section~\ref{sec:app}) of how the deletion
        characterisation reduces the global ``all b-invariant edges are
        forcing'' property to a finite family of local tests, underlying the
        dichotomy for near-bipartite bricks.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Matchings as fixed-point-free involutions}
\label{sec:model}

We fix a simple graph $G$ on vertex set $V$ with symmetric, irreflexive
adjacency $\Adj$.

\begin{definition}[Perfect matching]
A function $f:V\to V$ is a \emph{perfect matching} of $G$, written
$f \in \mathcal{M}(G)$, if: \textbf{(Involutive)} $f(f(v))=v$ for all $v$;
\textbf{(Fixed-point-free)} $f(v)\ne v$ for all $v$; and
\textbf{(Edge-respecting)} $v$ is adjacent to $f(v)$ for all $v$.
\end{definition}

Such an $f$ partitions $V$ into unordered pairs $\{v,f(v)\}$, each an edge; this
model is equivalent to the classical edge-set model but makes ``the partner of
$v$'' a first-class object.

\begin{definition}[Forcing edge]
For $u,v\in V$, the pair $(u,v)$ is \emph{forcing}, written $(u,v) \in \mathcal{F}(G)$,
if $u$ is adjacent to $v$ and there exists a \emph{unique} $f$ with $f \in \mathcal{M}(G)$
and $f(u)=v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Matching of the deleted graph]
For $u,v\in V$, a function $h:V\to V$ is a \emph{perfect matching of $G$ with
$u,v$ deleted}, written $h \in \mathcal{M}(G-u-v)$, if $h$ is involutive, $h(u)=u$,
$h(v)=v$, and for every $w\notin\{u,v\}$ we have $h(w)\ne w$, $w$ adjacent to
$h(w)$, and $h(w)\notin\{u,v\}$.
\end{definition}

Here $G-u-v$ is represented \emph{in place} on $V$: the deleted vertices are
parked as fixed points and every other vertex is matched, within the graph, to
a partner distinct from $u,v$.

\section{The interior-avoidance lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Interior avoidance]
\label{lem:avoid}
Let $f \in \mathcal{M}(G)$ and $f(u)=v$. Then for every $w$ with $w\ne u$ and $w\ne v$
we have $f(w)\ne u$ and $f(w)\ne v$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since $f$ is an involution, $f(u)=v$ gives $f(v)=u$. If $f(w)=u$, applying $f$
gives $w=f(u)=v$, contradicting $w\ne v$. If $f(w)=v$, then $w=f(v)=u$,
contradicting $w\ne u$.
\end{proof}

In matching language, $u$ and $v$ are already committed to each other, so no
third vertex can claim either; this is injectivity of the involution.

\section{The deletion characterisation}

Fix distinct $u,v$ (automatic when $uv$ is an edge, since $G$ is loopless).

\begin{definition}[Restriction and extension]
Define
\[
(\restrict f)(w)=
\begin{cases}
u & w=u,\\ v & w=v,\\ f(w) & \text{otherwise;}
\end{cases}
\qquad
(\extend h)(w)=
\begin{cases}
v & w=u,\\ u & w=v,\\ h(w) & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Restriction lands in the deleted graph]
\label{lem:restrict}
If $f \in \mathcal{M}(G)$, $f(u)=v$ and $u\ne v$, then $\restrict f \in \mathcal{M}(G-u-v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Involutivity of $\restrict f$ is checked by cases on $w\in\{u,v\}$, using
Lemma~\ref{lem:avoid} so that for interior $w$, $f(w)\notin\{u,v\}$ and is not
re-mapped. The fixed-point conditions at $u,v$ are immediate. For interior $w$
the four required facts follow from fixed-point-freeness, edge-respect, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:avoid}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Extension lands in $G$ through $uv$]
\label{lem:extend}
If $h \in \mathcal{M}(G-u-v)$ and $u$ is adjacent to $v$, then $\extend h \in \mathcal{M}(G)$
and $(\extend h)(u)=v$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By construction $(\extend h)(u)=v$. Involutivity is a case check: $u\mapsto
v\mapsto u$, and interior vertices use involutivity of $h$ with
$h(w)\notin\{u,v\}$. Fixed-point-freeness holds by $u\ne v$ and $h(w)\ne w$.
Edge-respect holds because $uv$ is an edge and $h$ is edge-respecting on the
interior.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Mutual inverses]
\label{lem:inv}
$\restrict(\extend h)=h$ for any deleted matching $h$, and
$\extend(\restrict f)=f$ for any matching $f$ with $f(u)=v$ (assuming $u\ne v$).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Pointwise case checks. For $\restrict(\extend h)$ the values at $u,v$ recover
$h(u)=u$, $h(v)=v$, and interior values pass through. For $\extend(\restrict
f)$ the swap at $u,v$ is restored from $f(u)=v$, $f(v)=u$, and interior values
pass through.
\end{proof}

Lemmas~\ref{lem:restrict}--\ref{lem:inv} say restriction and extension form a
bijection
\[
\{\,f:f \in \mathcal{M}(G),\ f(u)=v\,\}\ \xleftrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\
\{\,h:h \in \mathcal{M}(G-u-v)\,\},
\]
and a bijection carries ``exactly one element'' to ``exactly one element.''

\begin{theorem}[Deletion characterisation of forcing edges]
\label{thm:deletion}
For any graph $G$ and vertices $u,v$,
\[
(u,v) \in \mathcal{F}(G)\iff (u\text{ adjacent to }v)\ \wedge\
(\text{$G-u-v$ has a unique perfect matching}).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Let $f_0$ be the unique matching with $f_0(u)=v$. Then
$\restrict f_0$ is a deleted matching (Lemma~\ref{lem:restrict}). Any deleted
matching $h$ yields $\extend h$, a matching through $uv$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:extend}), so $\extend h=f_0$, whence
$h=\restrict(\extend h)=\restrict f_0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:inv}). Uniqueness follows.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $h_0$ be the unique deleted matching. Then $\extend h_0$ is a
matching through $uv$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:extend}). Any matching $f$ with $f(u)=v$
yields $\restrict f=h_0$, whence $f=\extend(\restrict f)=\extend h_0$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:inv}). Thus $(u,v)$ is forcing.
\end{proof}

The theorem needs no finiteness of $V$: it equates solution sets exactly.

\section{Companion results}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness principle for uniquely matchable graphs]
\label{thm:complete}
If $G$ has a unique perfect matching $f_0$, then for every vertex $v$ the edge
$\{v,f_0(v)\}$ is forcing: $(v,f_0 v) \in \mathcal{F}(G)$ holds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Adjacency of $v,f_0(v)$ is edge-respect. Any matching equals $f_0$ by
hypothesis, so a fortiori any matching sending $v$ to $f_0 v$ equals $f_0$;
uniqueness follows, with $f_0$ providing existence.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry of forcing]
\label{thm:sym}
For all $u,v$, $(u,v) \in \mathcal{F}(G)\iff(v,u) \in \mathcal{F}(G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Adjacency is symmetric, and for an involution $f$ the condition $f(u)=v$ is
equivalent to $f(v)=u$; the two definitions range over the same matchings.
\end{proof}

\section{Application: the dichotomy for near-bipartite bricks}
\label{sec:app}

\begin{definition}[Brick]
A \emph{brick} is a graph that is $3$-connected, \emph{bicritical} (for all
distinct $x,y$, $G-x-y$ has a perfect matching), and non-bipartite.
\end{definition}

The tight cut decomposition reduces every matching-covered graph to bricks and
braces, so bricks are the atoms of matching structure.

\begin{definition}[b-invariant edge]
An edge $e$ of a brick $G$ is \emph{b-invariant} if $G-e$ remains
matching-covered and its tight cut decomposition yields a single brick.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Near-bipartite graph]
A non-bipartite graph is \emph{near-bipartite} if some pair of edges
$\{e_1,e_2\}$ can be removed to leave a bipartite graph (meeting every odd
structure in the controlled way required in the brick setting). A near-bipartite
brick is ``one removable pair of edges away'' from being two-sided.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Forcing/near-bipartite dichotomy]
\label{thm:dichotomy}
Let $G$ be a brick not isomorphic to any of
\begin{itemize}
  \item $K_4$, the tetrahedron;
  \item $\Cbar$, the complement of the six-cycle; or
  \item the Petersen graph.
\end{itemize}
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
  \item Every b-invariant edge of $G$ is a forcing edge.
  \item $G$ is a near-bipartite brick belonging to the explicitly characterised
        family of near-bipartite bricks all of whose b-invariant edges are
        forcing.
\end{enumerate}
Apart from the three exceptions, ``all b-invariant edges are forcing'' holds
precisely for near-bipartite bricks in that family; the three exceptional
graphs satisfy (1) without being near-bipartite, which is why they are excluded.
\end{theorem}

\paragraph{How the deletion characterisation drives the proof.}
Statement~(1) quantifies over all b-invariant edges and asserts a global
uniqueness property for each. Theorem~\ref{thm:deletion} replaces each with a
local test: the b-invariant edge $uv$ is forcing iff $G-u-v$ is uniquely
matchable. A b-invariant edge \emph{fails} to be forcing exactly when $G-u-v$
has two distinct matchings, i.e.\ an alternating cycle avoiding $u,v$. Requiring
\emph{every} b-invariant edge to be forcing forbids a rich family of
alternating cycles; this scarcity is the combinatorial signature that forces the
brick into near-bipartite form. In $K_4$, $\Cbar$, and the Petersen graph, high
symmetry makes the relevant deletions uniquely matchable ``by accident'' despite
non-near-bipartiteness, isolating them as exceptions.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Algorithm A (Forcing test by deletion).}
Given $G$ and edge $uv$, delete $u,v$ and count perfect matchings of the
remainder, stopping at two; return ``forcing'' iff the count is exactly one
(Theorem~\ref{thm:deletion}).

\paragraph{Algorithm B (Forcing spectrum).}
Apply Algorithm A to every edge to return the complete set of forcing edges.

\paragraph{Algorithm C (Uniquely-matchable certificate).}
Decide whether a graph has a unique perfect matching, returning it as a
certificate; combined with Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}, a positive answer
certifies all matching edges forcing at once.

\section{Discussion and future work}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Deletion spectrum monotonicity.} Along a single/double ear
        decomposition of a matching-covered graph, the number of forcing edges
        is conjectured non-decreasing, with each double ear addition increasing
        it by at most the length of the shorter ear.
  \item \textbf{Spectral detection.} A brick with every internal edge forcing
        and a simple second-largest adjacency eigenvalue is conjectured
        near-bipartite.
  \item \textbf{Random cubic bricks.} In a random cubic brick on $2n$ vertices
        the fraction of forcing edges is conjectured to tend to $0$, with
        expected count $O(\log n)$.
  \item \textbf{Vertex-transitive all-forcing bricks.} Among vertex-transitive
        bricks, ``every edge forcing'' is conjectured to hold precisely for the
        three exceptional graphs.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

Modelling matchings as fixed-point-free involutions turns ``the matching
containing $uv$'' into an equation and endpoint deletion into an explicit
bijection, from which the deletion characterisation follows without finiteness
assumptions, along with the completeness principle and the symmetry of forcing.
The characterisation is load-bearing: it reduces the global property ``all
b-invariant edges of a brick are forcing'' to a finite family of local
unique-matching tests, on which the near-bipartite dichotomy -- up to the three
classical exceptions $K_4$, $\Cbar$, and the Petersen graph -- is established.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterator, List, Set, Tuple

# A graph is (vertices, edge set). Each edge is a frozenset of two vertices.
Vertex = int
Edge = FrozenSet[Vertex]
Graph = Tuple[Set[Vertex], Set[Edge]]
# A perfect matching is represented as a frozenset of its edges.
Matching = FrozenSet[Edge]


def make_graph(vertices: List[Vertex], edges: List[Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]]) -> Graph:
    """Build a simple graph from a vertex list and an edge list."""
    V: Set[Vertex] = set(vertices)
    E: Set[Edge] = {frozenset((a, b)) for a, b in edges if a != b}
    return (V, E)


def neighbors(g: Graph, v: Vertex) -> Set[Vertex]:
    """Return the set of neighbours of v."""
    V, E = g
    return {w for e in E if v in e for w in e if w != v}


def all_perfect_matchings(g: Graph) -> List[Matching]:
    """Enumerate all perfect matchings of g by backtracking.

    Returns a list of matchings, each a frozenset of edges covering every vertex
    exactly once. The empty graph has the single empty matching.
    """
    V, E = g
    verts: List[Vertex] = sorted(V)

    def backtrack(remaining: Tuple[Vertex, ...]) -> Iterator[Matching]:
        if not remaining:
            yield frozenset()
            return
        first = remaining[0]
        rest = remaining[1:]
        for other in rest:
            if frozenset((first, other)) in E:
                sub = tuple(x for x in rest if x != other)
                for m in backtrack(sub):
                    yield m | {frozenset((first, other))}

    return list(backtrack(tuple(verts)))


def delete_vertices(g: Graph, u: Vertex, v: Vertex) -> Graph:
    """Return the graph with vertices u and v (and incident edges) removed."""
    V, E = g
    Vn = {w for w in V if w != u and w != v}
    En = {e for e in E if u not in e and v not in e}
    return (Vn, En)


def is_forcing_bruteforce(g: Graph, u: Vertex, v: Vertex) -> bool:
    """Directly check: is uv an edge lying in exactly one perfect matching?"""
    V, E = g
    if frozenset((u, v)) not in E:
        return False
    containing = [m for m in all_perfect_matchings(g) if frozenset((u, v)) in m]
    return len(containing) == 1


def is_forcing_by_deletion(g: Graph, u: Vertex, v: Vertex) -> bool:
    """Deletion characterisation: uv is an edge and G - u - v has a UNIQUE PM."""
    V, E = g
    if frozenset((u, v)) not in E:
        return False
    deleted = delete_vertices(g, u, v)
    return len(all_perfect_matchings(deleted)) == 1


def forcing_edges(g: Graph) -> List[Edge]:
    """Return the complete forcing spectrum: all forcing edges of g."""
    V, E = g
    out: List[Edge] = []
    for e in E:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        if is_forcing_by_deletion(g, u, v):
            out.append(e)
    return out


def has_unique_perfect_matching(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """True iff g has exactly one perfect matching."""
    return len(all_perfect_matchings(g)) == 1


def fmt_edge(e: Edge) -> str:
    a, b = sorted(e)
    return f"{a}-{b}"


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Named graphs
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def path_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """Path on n vertices 0-1-2-...-(n-1)."""
    return make_graph(list(range(n)), [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)])


def cycle_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """Cycle on n vertices."""
    return make_graph(list(range(n)), [(i, (i + 1) % n) for i in range(n)])


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """Complete graph K_n."""
    return make_graph(list(range(n)), list(combinations(range(n), 2)))


def complement_of_c6() -> Graph:
    """Complement of the 6-cycle: an exceptional brick."""
    V = list(range(6))
    c6 = {frozenset(((i, (i + 1) % 6))) for i in range(6)}
    edges = [tuple(e) for e in (
        {frozenset(p) for p in combinations(V, 2)} - c6
    )]
    return make_graph(V, edges)


def petersen_graph() -> Graph:
    """The Petersen graph: outer 5-cycle, inner pentagram, spokes."""
    outer = [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    spokes = [(i, i + 5) for i in range(5)]
    inner = [(5 + i, 5 + (i + 2) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    return make_graph(list(range(10)), outer + spokes + inner)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_deletion_agrees_with_bruteforce() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. Deletion characterisation agrees with brute force")
    print("=" * 70)
    graphs = {
        "Path P4": path_graph(4),
        "Path P6": path_graph(6),
        "Cycle C4": cycle_graph(4),
        "Cycle C6": cycle_graph(6),
        "K4": complete_graph(4),
        "K6": complete_graph(6),
        "complement(C6)": complement_of_c6(),
        "Petersen": petersen_graph(),
    }
    for name, g in graphs.items():
        V, E = g
        ok = True
        for e in E:
            u, v = tuple(e)
            if is_forcing_bruteforce(g, u, v) != is_forcing_by_deletion(g, u, v):
                ok = False
                break
        status = "AGREE" if ok else "MISMATCH!"
        n_pm = len(all_perfect_matchings(g))
        print(f"  {name:16s}: {status:9s} (#perfect matchings = {n_pm})")
    print()


def demo_completeness_principle() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. Completeness principle: unique PM => every matching edge forcing")
    print("=" * 70)
    for name, g in [("Path P4", path_graph(4)), ("Path P6", path_graph(6))]:
        pms = all_perfect_matchings(g)
        assert len(pms) == 1, "expected a unique perfect matching"
        the_pm = pms[0]
        all_forcing = all(is_forcing_by_deletion(g, *tuple(e)) for e in the_pm)
        print(f"  {name:10s}: unique PM = "
              f"{{{', '.join(fmt_edge(e) for e in sorted(the_pm, key=lambda s: sorted(s)))}}}")
        print(f"             every matching edge forcing? {all_forcing}")
    print()


def demo_symmetry() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("3. Symmetry: forcing is a property of the undirected edge")
    print("=" * 70)
    g = path_graph(6)
    V, E = g
    ok = all(
        is_forcing_by_deletion(g, u, v) == is_forcing_by_deletion(g, v, u)
        for e in E for (u, v) in [tuple(e)]
    )
    print(f"  Path P6: forcing(u,v) == forcing(v,u) for all edges? {ok}")
    print()


def demo_forcing_spectrum() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("4. Forcing spectrum of several graphs")
    print("=" * 70)
    for name, g in [
        ("Path P6", path_graph(6)),
        ("Cycle C6", cycle_graph(6)),
        ("K4", complete_graph(4)),
        ("complement(C6)", complement_of_c6()),
        ("Petersen", petersen_graph()),
    ]:
        fe = forcing_edges(g)
        V, E = g
        print(f"  {name:16s}: {len(fe):2d}/{len(E):2d} edges forcing", end="")
        if fe:
            shown = ", ".join(fmt_edge(e) for e in sorted(fe, key=lambda s: sorted(s))[:8])
            print(f"   [{shown}]")
        else:

    print()


def demo_exceptional_bricks() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("5. The three classical exceptional bricks")
    print("=" * 70)
    for name, g in [
        ("K4 (tetrahedron)", complete_graph(4)),
        ("complement(C6)", complement_of_c6()),
        ("Petersen graph", petersen_graph()),
    ]:
        V, E = g
        n_pm = len(all_perfect_matchings(g))
        fe = forcing_edges(g)
        print(f"  {name:20s}: |V|={len(V)}, |E|={len(E)}, "
              f"#PM={n_pm}, forcing edges={len(fe)}")
    print("  (These graphs are the exceptions to the forcing/near-bipartite")
    print("   dichotomy for bricks.)")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    print()
    print("FORCING EDGES VIA ENDPOINT DELETION — numerical demonstration")
    print()
    demo_deletion_agrees_with_bruteforce()
    demo_completeness_principle()
    demo_symmetry()
    demo_forcing_spectrum()
    demo_exceptional_bricks()
    print("All demonstrations complete.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

/-!
# Forcing edges of perfect matchings, via fixed-point-free involutions

An edge `e = uv` of a graph `G` is a *forcing edge* if there is exactly one
perfect matching of `G` that contains it. Modelling perfect matchings as
fixed-point-free involutions `f : V -> V` (with `f u = v` meaning "the matching
pairs u with v"), the deletion characterisation states: `uv` is forcing iff it
is an edge and the graph with `u, v` deleted has a unique perfect matching.
-/

namespace ForcingEdges

open Function

variable {V : Type*}

def IsPM (G : SimpleGraph V) (f : V → V) : Prop :=
  Involutive f ∧ (∀ v, f v ≠ v) ∧ (∀ v, G.Adj v (f v))

def Forcing (G : SimpleGraph V) (u v : V) : Prop :=
  G.Adj u v ∧ ∃! f, IsPM G f ∧ f u = v

def IsPMdel (G : SimpleGraph V) (u v : V) (h : V → V) : Prop :=
  Involutive h ∧ h u = u ∧ h v = v ∧
    ∀ w, w ≠ u → w ≠ v → (h w ≠ w ∧ G.Adj w (h w) ∧ h w ≠ u ∧ h w ≠ v)

/-- In a perfect matching containing uv, no interior vertex is matched to u or v. -/
theorem IsPM.apply_ne {G : SimpleGraph V} {f : V → V} (hf : IsPM G f) {u v : V}
    (huv : f u = v) {w : V} (hwu : w ≠ u) (hwv : w ≠ v) :
    f w ≠ u ∧ f w ≠ v := by sorry

/-- Main theorem: the deletion characterisation of forcing edges. -/
theorem forcing_iff_unique_deletion [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (u v : V) :
    Forcing G u v ↔ G.Adj u v ∧ ∃! h, IsPMdel G u v h := by sorry

/-- If G has a unique perfect matching, every one of its edges is forcing. -/
theorem uniquePM_all_forcing {G : SimpleGraph V} {f₀ : V → V} (hpm : IsPM G f₀)
    (huniq : ∀ g, IsPM G g → g = f₀) (v : V) : Forcing G v (f₀ v) := by sorry

end ForcingEdges

  "future_directions": "# Future Directions — Forcing edges, deletion, and near-bipartite bricks

These conjectures grow out of the deletion characterisation of forcing edges
(an edge uv lies in a unique perfect matching exactly when removing u and v
leaves a graph with a unique perfect matching) and the two obstruction lemmas
(distinct matchings through an edge prevent forcing).

## 1. The deletion spectrum of a matching-covered graph is monotone under ear decompositions

**Conjecture.** For a matching-covered graph built up by a sequence of single and
double ear additions, the number of forcing edges is non-decreasing along the
decomposition, and each double ear addition increases it by at most the length of
the shorter ear.

The key insight is that adding an ear can only *merge* previously distinct
alternating routes, never create new ones through an old edge, so the "two
distinct matchings through an edge" obstruction can only be resolved, not
introduced, as the graph grows. Why now? The deletion characterisation reduces the
global forcing count to a purely local, per-edge test, which turns the ear
decomposition into a tractable induction on which the monotonicity can finally be
pinned down quantitatively.

## 2. Forcing edges detect near-bipartiteness among bricks with a spectral gap

**Conjecture.** A brick in which every strictly internal edge is forcing, and
whose adjacency matrix has a simple second-largest eigenvalue, is near-bipartite.

The key insight is that "every edge forcing" forbids short alternating cycles,
which in turn caps the multiplicity of extremal eigenvalues; a single spectral gap
then rigidly fixes the two colour classes that a near-bipartite structure requires.
Why now? The deletion characterisation gives a clean combinatorial certificate for
"no alternating cycle through an edge", which is exactly the hypothesis a spectral
argument needs as input, making the bridge between forcing edges and eigenvalue
multiplicity concrete for the first time.

## 3. Almost all edges of a random cubic brick are non-forcing

**Conjecture.** In a uniformly random cubic (3-regular) brick on 2n vertices,
the fraction of forcing edges tends to 0 as n → ∞, and in fact the expected
number of forcing edges is O(log n).

The key insight is that a forcing edge requires its two-vertex deletion to leave a
*uniquely* matchable remainder, an event that becomes exponentially unlikely once
the remainder is a dense expander with many alternating cycles. Why now? The
reduction of forcing to a unique-matching property of a deleted subgraph lets one
import the well-developed first-moment machinery for counting perfect matchings in
random regular graphs, which previously had no clean hook into forcing questions.

## 4. The three classical exceptions are exactly the vertex-transitive all-forcing bricks

**Conjecture.** Among vertex-transitive bricks, the property "every edge is
forcing" holds precisely for the three small exceptional graphs (the tetrahedron
K4, the complement of the six-cycle, and the Petersen graph). Their high symmetry,
which forces uniform behaviour under two-vertex deletion, is conjecturally exactly
what singles them out.

    "demo": """"
demo.py — Forcing edges via endpoint deletion.

This self-contained script demonstrates the central results of the accompanying
paper on *forcing edges* of perfect matchings:

  * A perfect matching is modelled as a fixed-point-free involution on the
    vertex set: a pairing rule f with f(f(v)) = v, f(v) != v, and {v, f(v)} an
    edge for every vertex v.

  * An edge uv is a FORCING EDGE if exactly one perfect matching contains it.

  * DELETION CHARACTERISATION (main theorem): uv is forcing  <=>  uv is an edge
    AND the graph with both u and v deleted has a UNIQUE perfect matching.

  * COMPLETENESS PRINCIPLE: if a graph has a unique perfect matching, every one
    of its matching edges is forcing.

  * SYMMETRY: forcing is a property of the undirected edge (uv forcing <=> vu).

The script verifies the deletion characterisation against brute force on several
graphs, and inspects the three classical exceptional bricks (the tetrahedron
K4, the complement of the six-cycle, and the Petersen graph).

Pure standard library; run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterator, List, Set, Tuple

# A graph is (vertices, edge set). Each edge is a frozenset of two vertices.
Vertex = int
Edge = FrozenSet[Vertex]
Graph = Tuple[Set[Vertex], Set[Edge]]
# A perfect matching is represented as a frozenset of its edges.
Matching = FrozenSet[Edge]


def make_graph(vertices: List[Vertex], edges: List[Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]]) -> Graph:
    """Build a simple graph from a vertex list and an edge list."""
    V: Set[Vertex] = set(vertices)
    E: Set[Edge] = {frozenset((a, b)) for a, b in edges if a != b}
    return (V, E)


def neighbors(g: Graph, v: Vertex) -> Set[Vertex]:
    """Return the set of neighbours of v."""
    V, E = g
    return {w for e in E if v in e for w in e if w != v}


def all_perfect_matchings(g: Graph) -> List[Matching]:
    """Enumerate all perfect matchings of g by backtracking.

    Returns a list of matchings, each a frozenset of edges covering every vertex
    exactly once. The empty graph has the single empty matching.
    """
    V, E = g
    verts: List[Vertex] = sorted(V)

    def backtrack(remaining: Tuple[Vertex, ...]) -> Iterator[Matching]:
        if not remaining:
            yield frozenset()
            return
        first = remaining[0]
        rest = remaining[1:]
        for other in rest:
            if frozenset((first, other)) in E:
                sub = tuple(x for x in rest if x != other)
                for m in backtrack(sub):
                    yield m | {frozenset((first, other))}

    return list(backtrack(tuple(verts)))


def delete_vertices(g: Graph, u: Vertex, v: Vertex) -> Graph:
    """Return the graph with vertices u and v (and incident edges) removed."""
    V, E = g
    Vn = {w for w in V if w != u and w != v}
    En = {e for e in E if u not in e and v not in e}
    return (Vn, En)


def is_forcing_bruteforce(g: Graph, u: Vertex, v: Vertex) -> bool:
    """Directly check: is uv an edge lying in exactly one perfect matching?"""
    V, E = g
    if frozenset((u, v)) not in E:
        return False
    containing = [m for m in all_perfect_matchings(g) if frozenset((u, v)) in m]
    return len(containing) == 1


def is_forcing_by_deletion(g: Graph, u: Vertex, v: Vertex) -> bool:
    """Deletion characterisation: uv is an edge and G - u - v has a UNIQUE PM."""
    V, E = g
    if frozenset((u, v)) not in E:
        return False
    deleted = delete_vertices(g, u, v)
    return len(all_perfect_matchings(deleted)) == 1


def forcing_edges(g: Graph) -> List[Edge]:
    """Return the complete forcing spectrum: all forcing edges of g."""
    V, E = g
    out: List[Edge] = []
    for e in E:
        u, v = tuple(e)
        if is_forcing_by_deletion(g, u, v):
            out.append(e)
    return out


def has_unique_perfect_matching(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """True iff g has exactly one perfect matching."""
    return len(all_perfect_matchings(g)) == 1


def fmt_edge(e: Edge) -> str:
    a, b = sorted(e)
    return f"{a}-{b}"


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Named graphs
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def path_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """Path on n vertices 0-1-2-...-(n-1)."""
    return make_graph(list(range(n)), [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)])


def cycle_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """Cycle on n vertices."""
    return make_graph(list(range(n)), [(i, (i + 1) % n) for i in range(n)])


def complete_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    """Complete graph K_n."""
    return make_graph(list(range(n)), list(combinations(range(n), 2)))


def complement_of_c6() -> Graph:
    """Complement of the 6-cycle: an exceptional brick."""
    V = list(range(6))
    c6 = {frozenset(((i, (i + 1) % 6))) for i in range(6)}
    edges = [tuple(e) for e in (
        {frozenset(p) for p in combinations(V, 2)} - c6
    )]
    return make_graph(V, edges)


def petersen_graph() -> Graph:
    """The Petersen graph: outer 5-cycle, inner pentagram, spokes."""
    outer = [(i, (i + 1) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    spokes = [(i, i + 5) for i in range(5)]
    inner = [(5 + i, 5 + (i + 2) % 5) for i in range(5)]
    return make_graph(list(range(10)), outer + spokes + inner)

# Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_deletion_agrees_with_bruteforce() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. Deletion characterisation agrees with brute force")
    print("=" * 70)
    graphs = {
        "Path P4": path_graph(4),
        "Path P6": path_graph(6),
        "Cycle C4": cycle_graph(4),
        "Cycle C6": cycle_graph(6),
        "K4": complete_graph(4),
        "K6": complete_graph(6),
        "complement(C6)": complement_of_c6(),
        "Petersen": petersen_graph(),

        print(f"             every matching edge forcing? {all_forcing}")

concept.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back
concept.concept_description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.
